This replaces the arg-packed SVC_IPC_REGISTER_REQ, whose 16-byte name consumed all four args and forced the reply onto the serve endpoint (a latent races that deadlocked boot once PM stopped busy-polling).  |
| `SVC_IPC_LOOKUP_CLASS_REQ` | 0x223 | req | Class-based discovery (see docs/architecture/09-process-and-ipc.md). SUBSCRIBE_CLASS: receive existence events for a class. req  arg0=notify_endpoint (where SVC_IPC_CLASS_EVENT is delivered), arg1=buffer_id (class name NUL-terminated at offset 0); resp SVC_IPC_SUBSCRIBE_CLASS_RESP arg0=0. CLASS_EVENT is pushed to a subscriber's notify_endpoint on add/remove/die: arg0=SVC_CLASS_EVENT_* arg1=instance arg2=endpoint arg3=pid.  |
| `SVC_IPC_SUBSCRIBE_CLASS_REQ` | 0x224 | req |  |
| `SVC_IPC_UNREGISTER_CLASS_REQ` | 0x225 | req | Retire a class registration the sender itself made. req  arg0=buffer_id (class name NUL-terminated at offset 0), arg1=instance; resp SVC_IPC_UNREGISTER_CLASS_RESP arg0=0.  The class name travels in a buffer for the same reason LOOKUP_CLASS and SUBSCRIBE_CLASS carry theirs there: a name is up to 16 bytes and would consume every argument word.  Subscribers see SVC_CLASS_EVENT with arg0=SVC_CLASS_EVENT_REMOVE, carrying the endpoint and pid the provider HAD -- indistinguishable from the event fired when an owner dies, deliberately: a subscriber wants to stop addressing an endpoint, and why it went is not its business.  Only the OWNER may retire a registration. A registration is a claim on (class, instance), and letting another context drop one would let anything unpublish a device it does not own -- the impersonation the register path already refuses, which has to be refused at both ends or it is not refused at all. Retiring one nobody holds, or one held by somebody else, fails the same way: it is not yours to retire.  |
| `SVC_IPC_SUBSCRIBE_NAME_REQ` | 0x226 | req | Receive existence events for one service NAME. req  arg0=buffer_id arg1=byte_offset arg2=size of a svc_name_subscribe_desc_t in the caller's own transfer buffer (notify_endpoint, cookie, name); resp SVC_IPC_SUBSCRIBE_NAME_RESP arg0=0.  SVC_IPC_NAME_EVENT is then pushed to notify_endpoint whenever the name is BOUND: first registered, re-pointed at a different endpoint by its owner, or claimed by a new owner after the previous one died. A re-registration that changes nothing is not an event.  Subscribing does not replay a binding that already exists. A caller that wants "the provider, now or when it appears" subscribes FIRST and looks the name up SECOND; the reverse order loses a registration that lands between the two.  The subscription is keyed by (notify_endpoint, cookie), which must be the caller's: the cookie is the subscriber's own tag, echoed in every event, so one endpoint can watch several names and tell them apart. Subscribing an existing key again re-targets it at the new name. notify_endpoint must belong to the caller.  |

Idempotent: dropping a key that is not subscribed succeeds, so a caller tearing down after a lost reply cannot fail. Only the owner of notify_endpoint may drop it.  |

## block (0x300–0x3FF)

| Opcode | Value | Kind | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `BLOCK_IPC_READ_REQ` | 0x300 | req | Read sectors, described by a wasmos_block_request_t in a buffer the CALLER owns and has borrowed to this endpoint. arg0=buffer_id arg1=byte_offset arg2=size arg3=reserved(0).  The request names its own target device, its 64-bit LBA, and where the data goes (see BLOCK_DST_* in abi/constants.yaml). None of that fits in four argument words, which is why they no longer carry it: the packed form forced a 32-bit LBA, inferred the target from the sender's endpoint, and needed a separate opcode for a transfer-buffer destination.  A caller acquires and borrows ONE buffer per operation and reuses it for every request in that operation, writing a fresh request into its own slot; the buffer is not acquired per transfer.  On success: BLOCK_IPC_READ_RESP, arg1 = sectors transferred, which may be fewer than asked. On failure: BLOCK_IPC_ERROR, arg0 = reason.  |
| `BLOCK_IPC_WRITE_REQ` | 0x301 | req | Write sectors, described by a wasmos_block_request_t exactly as BLOCK_IPC_READ_REQ describes a read: arg0=buffer_id arg1=byte_offset arg2=size arg3=reserved(0). The destination fields name the SOURCE of the data here; the direction is the opcode's.  On success: BLOCK_IPC_WRITE_RESP, arg1 = sectors transferred. On failure: BLOCK_IPC_ERROR, arg0 = reason.  |
| `BLOCK_IPC_IDENTIFY_REQ` | 0x302 | req | Ask a backend to describe one of its devices into a buffer the CALLER owns. arg0 = the device's `block` CLASS INSTANCE, arg1 = buffer_id. Answered with BLOCK_IPC_IDENTIFY_RESP.  The caller acquires the buffer, borrows it to this endpoint with WRITE, and releases it when done -- the ownership model of docs/architecture/12-dma-transfers.md, where the client holds the lifecycle and the server is a transient grantee. A backend lending its OWN buffer instead would have to keep it alive for every client that ever asked, track who already holds a grant, and never rewrite it while lent; none of which it can do correctly, because a borrow is held per context and nothing tells a server when a client is finished.  The instance rather than a unit, because that is the only name a client has: it found the provider by looking up the class, several instances of which may share one endpoint (an ATA controller registers one per drive). The instance is an opaque fingerprint of a canonical id, so nothing can be decoded out of it -- but the backend computed those fingerprints itself and can match one back to its own device. arg0 = 0 means "the only device you serve", which a single-disk backend may take as read.  IDENTIFY does not claim the device: reading a disk's geometry is not exclusive use, and requiring a claim made a mounted disk unqueryable, which defeats discovering it by class in the first place.  |
| `BLOCK_IPC_FLUSH_REQ` | 0x304 | req | Commit everything already written to durable media, so a caller that orders its writes can rely on that order surviving power loss. arg0..arg3 reserved (must be zero). Ordering a request after a reply only guarantees the DEVICE saw them in that order; a volatile write cache may still lose the earlier ones. A journal barrier (docs/WFS_WASMOS_FILE_SYSTEM.md section 14, steps 2, 4 and 6) is exactly that guarantee and needs this. A device with no volatile write cache answers success without doing anything, because for it the guarantee already holds. On success: BLOCK_IPC_FLUSH_RESP. On failure: BLOCK_IPC_ERROR, arg0 = reason.  |
| `BLOCK_IPC_READ_RESP` | 0x380 | resp |  |
| `BLOCK_IPC_WRITE_RESP` | 0x381 | resp |  |
| `BLOCK_IPC_IDENTIFY_RESP` | 0x382 | resp | The answer to BLOCK_IPC_IDENTIFY_REQ: a wasmos_block_descriptor_t written into the caller's own buffer at offset 0. arg0=0 on success, arg1=bytes written. The caller already knows the buffer_id -- it acquired it -- so the reply names only how much is there.  The descriptor is written FRESH on every call, so it is the device's state at reply time rather than a snapshot the backend published earlier and may since have outgrown.  Geometry that used to travel in the arguments -- sector count, unit -- is in the descriptor, together with everything a caller now matches on: canonical_id, scheme, fs_type, the GPT identity fields, and the LBA window. Callers read fields; they do not decode packed words.  |
| `BLOCK_IPC_FLUSH_RESP` | 0x383 | resp |  |
| `BLOCK_IPC_ERROR` | 0x3FF | error |  |

## fs (0x400–0x4FF)

| Opcode | Value | Kind | Description |

| `FS_IPC_OPEN_REQ` | 0x400 | req |  |
| `FS_IPC_READ_REQ` | 0x401 | req |  |
| `FS_IPC_CLOSE_REQ` | 0x402 | req |  |
| `FS_IPC_STAT_REQ` | 0x403 | req | Report a path's size in the reply's arg0 and its POSIX-shaped mode in arg1.  The mode MUST carry the file TYPE bits (S_IFDIR 0x4000, S_IFREG 0x8000, S_IFLNK 0xA000), not permission bits alone. Two consumers read the type out of it and have nothing else to read: libc's S_ISDIR, and fs-manager when it validates a chdir target. A backend that reports permissions alone describes every directory it holds as a regular file.  A backend must answer for its own mount ROOT, which typically has no on-disk entry describing it: a volume whose root cannot be stat'd is a mount nobody can stand at the top of.  |
| `FS_IPC_READY_REQ` | 0x404 | req |  |
| `FS_IPC_SEEK_REQ` | 0x405 | req |  |
| `FS_IPC_WRITE_REQ` | 0x406 | req |  |

| `FS_IPC_RMDIR_REQ` | 0x409 | req |  |
| `FS_IPC_READDIR_REQ` | 0x410 | req | List a directory, streaming one FS_IPC_STREAM frame per entry and terminating with FS_IPC_RESP.  The two legs carry different things. From a CLIENT it names no path: fs-manager owns the working directory, so a client supplying one would have to know a path fs-manager is the authority on. To the BACKEND it carries the mount-relative path in fs-manager's own buffer -- arg0 = length, arg2 = buffer id, arg3 = the grant -- exactly like every other path op.  A backend therefore holds NO working directory. It previously listed whichever directory it last been told to stand in, which cost a CHDIR round trip before every listing and made the result depend on the previous request rather than on this one.  |
| `FS_IPC_CHDIR_REQ` | 0x412 | req | Change the working directory. CLIENT to fs-manager ONLY: fs-manager owns the working directory as a full VFS path and resolves every client path against it, so a backend that also kept one would hold a second copy of state it is not the authority on.  fs-manager validates the target with FS_IPC_STAT_REQ and reads the type out of the reported mode. It does not send a backend a CHDIR; nothing does.  arg0 = path length, arg2 = the client's buffer, arg3 = the grant. A zero length names the VFS root. The reply reports the resolved absolute path in arg1, since arg0 carries the status.  |
| `FS_IPC_READ_APP_REQ` | 0x413 | req |  |
| `FS_IPC_READ_PATH_REQ` | 0x414 | req |  |
| `FS_IPC_RENAME_REQ` | 0x415 | req |  |
| `FS_IPC_RESP` | 0x480 | resp |  |
| `FS_IPC_STREAM` | 0x481 | resp |  |

## fs_manager (0x420–0x4A5)

| Opcode | Value | Kind | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `FSMGR_IPC_BACKEND_INFO_REQ` | 0x420 | req | fs-manager -> backend pull: report kind/fs-type/mount/device into a buffer the CALLER owns. arg0 = buffer_id. Reply RESP packs arg0=kind, arg1=fs_type, arg2=mount_name_len, arg3=device_id_len. Backends are discovered via svc class FSMGR_BACKEND_CLASS, not a push, so fs-manager rebuilds its backend set from the registry on (re)start.  The buffer carries BOTH strings, the mount name at offset 0 and the device's canonical id immediately after it at offset arg2. Neither is NUL-terminated there; the two lengths delimit them.  arg3 == 0 means this filesystem sits on no block device -- an absence, not an unknown -- and `mount` then names no device for it. A backend that HAS one reports the id it was spawned with, because the backend is the authority: it is the string it fingerprinted to find its block server. fs-manager asking device-manager instead cannot work, and the retired backend_refresh_boot_meta is the proof -- it was a synchronous query to a service that is itself blocked waiting on fs-manager during bring-up.  A backend MUST name its mount: arg2 > 0 always. Nothing else knows where a backend belongs -- a block backend is told by the rule that spawned it and a pseudo-filesystem knows from what it is -- so a default on the fs-manager side could only be a guess, and a guess that named one filesystem would have to name every future one. A reply with arg2 == 0 is malformed and the backend is not registered.  fs-manager acquires the buffer, borrows it to the backend with WRITE, and releases it once the reply is read -- the ownership model of docs/architecture/12-dma-transfers.md, where the client of an exchange holds the lifecycle and the server is a transient grantee. The backend writes its mount name at offset 0 and owns nothing.  A backend lending its OWN buffer here instead is refused ALREADY_BORROWED on the second pull, and fs-manager pulls each backend more than once (class lookup plus the ADD event). It also could never release it: a borrow is held per context and nothing tells a server when a client is finished.  arg0 `kind` is FSMGR_BACKEND_BLOCK or FSMGR_BACKEND_PSEUDO: it separates a backend served from a block device from one served from anything else, and carries NO filesystem identity, so every block-backed backend reports the same value whatever it mounts. arg1 `fs_type` is the FS_TYPE_* the backend serves and is the only field that answers "which filesystem". A backend that sits on no block device names itself too -- initfs reports FS_TYPE_INITFS -- so a pseudo-filesystem is a value in that enum rather than a special case wherever a mount is named; FS_TYPE_UNKNOWN means the backend named nothing. Deriving a filesystem from `kind` reports every mounted volume as FAT.  |
| `FSMGR_IPC_CLONE_CWD_REQ` | 0x421 | req |  |
| `FSMGR_IPC_QUERY_MOUNTS_REQ` | 0x422 | req |  |
| `FSMGR_IPC_UNMOUNT_REQ` | 0x423 | req | Remove a mount, named by its absolute mount PATH. arg0 = path length, arg2 = the client's buffer holding it, arg3 = the client's grant -- the transport FS_IPC_CHDIR_REQ uses, and for the same reason: a path can grow, so it does not belong in the four argument words.  Refused with WASMOS_ERR_FS_MOUNT_BUSY while anything still stands in the mount: a deeper mount inside it, or an open file on it. The root is therefore normally busy, because every other mount is inside it, rather than by a rule written for the root.  A client whose WORKING DIRECTORY is under the mount is NOT counted, though Linux refuses on exactly that. fs-manager never releases a client's state -- nothing tells it a client died -- so a working directory recorded by a process that has since exited would refuse the unmount forever. See docs/TASKS.md for the mechanism that has to exist before the rule can be added.  The mount POINT is left in place. It is a directory in the covering filesystem, and removing it would delete state the mount only borrowed; an empty directory left behind is harmless, and the next mount at that path reuses it. What DOES come back is whatever the covering filesystem held underneath, because routing stops preferring the mount -- the other half of shadowing.  The backend is told to shut down (WASMOS_IPC_SHUTDOWN_REQ) before it is dropped, so a filesystem holding dirty state gets the chance every orderly teardown gets; WFS writes its clean mark there. A backend that does not answer is dropped anyway: the namespace is fs-manager's to decide, and a wedged driver must not be able to keep a mount alive.  |
| `FSMGR_IPC_MOUNT_REQ` | 0x424 | req | Establish a mount. arg0 = descriptor length, arg2 = the client's buffer holding the descriptor, arg3 = the client's grant.  The descriptor is whitespace-separated `key=value` text, not a packed struct, because what a filesystem needs to be placed differs per type and the set grows:    type=<tmpfs\|fat\|wfs>   which filesystem to place. Required.   mount=<absolute path>  where it goes. Required.   source=<canonical block id>                          which volume backs it, e.g. `block:ata:0p1`.                          Required for every type that has a device;                          refused for one that has none.  fs-manager does not implement a filesystem: it SPAWNS the driver for `type` and hands it `mount=` (and `id=<source>` for a disk-backed one) as startup arguments, which is the same contract a device-manager rule's ENV{MOUNT} uses. Placement is therefore one mechanism whether a mount comes from a boot rule or from this request.  `source` is required rather than optional for a disk-backed type even though the drivers can self-select a volume: a mount that picks its own device is not the mount the caller asked for, and there is no way for the caller to find out which one it got.  On success the mount IS in the table -- fs-manager re-runs backend discovery before replying rather than waiting for the class event to arrive on its own, so a caller that immediately queries the mount table sees it. arg1 of the reply carries the driver's pid.  Refusals: WASMOS_ERR_FS_MOUNT_EXISTS when that path is already a mount (a mount is not stacked on another at the same path); WASMOS_ERR_FS_MOUNT_FSTYPE for a type with no driver, or for a type/source combination that cannot be satisfied; WASMOS_ERR_FS_NOT_ABSOLUTE for a path that is not absolute. A driver that fails to reach readiness is reported as WASMOS_ERR_FS_NOT_READY -- nothing is left in the table in that case, because the entry only appears when the backend registers.  |
| `FSMGR_IPC_MOUNT_WAIT_REQ` | 0x425 | req | Answer once a mount exists at a path: a milestone from the owner of the mount table. The request is a wasmos_fsmgr_mount_wait_desc_t in a transfer buffer the caller owns and has lent READ to fs-manager: arg0=buffer_id arg1=offset arg2=size. fs-manager copies the path out at once, so the caller may release the buffer after the reply.  The reply, FSMGR_IPC_MOUNT_WAIT_RESP arg0=0, is DEFERRED: it is sent when a backend serving exactly that mount path registers, or at once if one already has. A mount exists from the moment its backend registers, whoever started it -- a device-manager rule (the boot volume) or FSMGR_IPC_MOUNT_REQ. There is no timeout here: the caller bounds its own wait. A waiter whose endpoint's process ends is dropped.  Refusals (FS_IPC_ERROR): WASMOS_ERR_FS_BUFFER when the descriptor cannot be read, WASMOS_ERR_FS_BAD_ARGS for a wrong version or a path length past FSMGR_MOUNT_WAIT_PATH_MAX, WASMOS_ERR_FS_NOT_ABSOLUTE for a relative path, WASMOS_ERR_FS_NO_CLIENT_SLOT when every waiter slot is taken.  |
| `FSMGR_IPC_BACKEND_INFO_RESP` | 0x4A0 | resp |  |
| `FSMGR_IPC_CLONE_CWD_RESP` | 0x4A1 | resp |  |
| `FSMGR_IPC_QUERY_MOUNTS_RESP` | 0x4A2 | resp |  |
| `FSMGR_IPC_UNMOUNT_RESP` | 0x4A3 | resp |  |
| `FSMGR_IPC_MOUNT_RESP` | 0x4A4 | resp |  |
| `FSMGR_IPC_MOUNT_WAIT_RESP` | 0x4A5 | resp | arg0 = 0: a mount exists at the path that was waited for. |

The value stays reserved rather than being reused.  |

ATTACH (once) hands the driver a borrowed grid buffer to map; BLIT_GRID (per repaint) tells it to render cols*rows fbtext_blit_cell_t entries from that buffer.  |

Fire-and-forget (request_id 0); the driver renders BLIT_GRID at the new column count from then on, so the receiver re-lays its grids out before its next blit.  |
| `FBTEXT_IPC_PRESENTER_REQ` | 0x60D | req | display presenter -> driver: the sender presents the scanout and must be told what is drawn (DISPLAY_IPC_FLUSH_REQ, subsystem `display`). The driver accepts it only from the endpoint the service registry has bound to "display", which it asks before answering; the answer is therefore deferred. It then owns its own flush descriptor buffer and lends it READ to the sender; a later accepted PRESENTER_REQ (a restarted presenter) replaces the previous one. No arguments; RESP when the loan is made, ERROR (arg0 = packed WASMOS_ERR_*) when it is not -- WASMOS_ERR_DISPLAY_NOT_PRESENTER for a sender that is not "display".  |

Without this doorbell an idle vt drains only on the next unrelated message, which strands klog on screen while the system is quiet.  |

## device_manager (0x901–0x982)

| Opcode | Value | Kind | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `DEVMGR_PCI_SCAN_DONE` | 0x901 | resp |  |
| `DEVMGR_QUERY_MOUNT_REQ` | 0x902 | req |  |
| `DEVMGR_PUBLISH_BLOCK_DEVICE` | 0x903 | req | Announce one block device to the device-manager inventory as a wasmos_block_descriptor_t held in a transfer buffer the publisher has borrowed to this endpoint. arg0=buffer_id arg1=byte_offset arg2=descriptor_size arg3=reserved(0).  Each device occupies its own offset, so the publisher never overwrites a descriptor the receiver has not read yet and no acknowledgement is needed -- the same discipline DEVMGR_PUBLISH_DEVICE_DESC uses.  The descriptor's canonical_id is the device's IDENTITY and the inventory keys on it. backend and unit are attributes of the device rather than its name: the unit is BACKEND-LOCAL, since ATA numbers its drives 0 and 1 while a virtio-blk device numbers itself by bus position. Publishing without a backend leaves the record BLOCK_BACKEND_UNKNOWN, which no `DRIVER==` rule matches.  A descriptor whose version is not BLOCK_DESCRIPTOR_VERSION is dropped rather than partially read; see WASMOS_ERR_BLOCK_DEV_DESCRIPTOR_VERSION.  |
| `DEVMGR_ACPI_SCAN_DONE` | 0x905 | resp | acpi-bus has published every device it found (DEVMGR_PUBLISH_ACPI_DEVICE_DESC); sent once, after the last one.  |
| `DEVMGR_PUBLISH_DEVICE_DESC` | 0x906 | req | Publish one enumerated PCI function as a wasmos_pci_device_desc_t held in a transfer buffer the publisher has borrowed to this endpoint. arg0=buffer_id arg1=byte_offset arg2=descriptor_size arg3=reserved(0). Each device occupies its own offset, so the publisher never overwrites a descriptor the receiver has not read yet and no acknowledgement is needed. Supersedes DEVMGR_PUBLISH_DEVICE (retired), whose four argument words could not describe six BARs and the capability offsets.  |
| `DEVMGR_PUBLISH_VOLUME` | 0x907 | req | Announce one VOLUME to the device-manager inventory as a wasmos_volume_descriptor_t held in a transfer buffer the publisher has borrowed to this endpoint. arg0=buffer_id arg1=byte_offset arg2=descriptor_size arg3=reserved(0).  Same discipline as DEVMGR_PUBLISH_BLOCK_DEVICE: one offset per volume, so a publisher never overwrites a descriptor the receiver has not read yet, and no acknowledgement is owed.  A volume is what can be MOUNTED, which the `block` inventory cannot say: a partition-table entry may hold no filesystem and a disk with no table may hold one. The two inventories are therefore separate rather than one with a flag -- a rule matching SUBSYSTEM=="volume" is asking a different question from one matching SUBSYSTEM=="block".  The descriptor names its backing device by CLASS INSTANCE, not by id. A consumer that needs the id resolves it through the block inventory, which is where the publisher of that id already put it; carrying a second copy here would be a second place that can disagree.  A descriptor whose version is not VOLUME_DESCRIPTOR_VERSION is dropped rather than partially read.  |
| `DEVMGR_UNPUBLISH_BLOCK_DEVICE` | 0x908 | req | Retire one block device from the inventory. The device's canonical_id is the identity and travels in a transfer buffer the caller owns: arg0=buffer_id arg1=byte_offset arg2=length, NUL-terminated. Answered with DEVMGR_UNPUBLISH_RESP.  The id rather than a derived key, for the same reason the publish path keys on it: a unit collides across backends, and this service never probed the bus so it is in no position to invent a better name. Too long for four argument words, hence the buffer.  ANSWERED, unlike the publish opcodes, which are fire-and-forget. A publisher that is told nothing simply tried; a caller retiring a device is about to stop serving it, and has to know whether the inventory agreed.  Retiring an id nobody published is refused rather than ignored: a caller that retires twice would otherwise read the second as having retired something.  A retire does NOT consider whether something has the device mounted. This inventory is rule-matching state and no mount addresses it, so retiring a record cannot disturb a running filesystem; the device manager is also never told about an unmount, so it could not answer the question even if it were the right place to ask. The caller unmounts first, and fs-manager is what refuses a busy unmount.  Queued rules the record armed are DISARMED, because a rule that had matched it would otherwise go on to mount a device the inventory no longer has. A rule that already spawned is left alone: its filesystem is running, and this retires an inventory record, not a mount.  |
| `DEVMGR_UNPUBLISH_VOLUME` | 0x909 | req | Retire one VOLUME from the inventory, by canonical_id in a caller-owned transfer buffer: arg0=buffer_id arg1=byte_offset arg2=length. Answered with DEVMGR_UNPUBLISH_RESP.  Same terms as DEVMGR_UNPUBLISH_BLOCK_DEVICE. What makes this one necessary is that a volume can cease to exist while its disk does not: writing a partition table over an unpartitioned disk ends the whole-disk volume, because the partitions are the volumes from then on.  |
| `DEVMGR_PUBLISH_ACPI_DEVICE_DESC` | 0x90A | req | Publish one ACPI namespace device as a wasmos_acpi_device_desc_t held in a transfer buffer the publisher (acpi-bus) owns and has borrowed to this endpoint for reading. arg0=buffer_id arg1=byte_offset arg2=descriptor_size arg3=reserved(0). Each device occupies its own offset, so the publisher never overwrites a descriptor the receiver has not read yet and no acknowledgement is needed. The publisher keeps the buffer, and so stays resident, for as long as the receiver may still read it.  |
| `DEVMGR_UNPUBLISH_RESP` | 0x982 | resp | arg0 = 0, or a packed error code: the id is malformed, or is not in the inventory. |
| `DEVMGR_MOUNT_INFO` | 0x980 | resp |  |
| `DEVMGR_QUERY_DONE` | 0x981 | resp |  |

| `GFX_IPC_GET_SURFACE_SPEC` | 0x210 | req | Reply the CONSTRAINTS a surface must satisfy for `window_id`; allocates nothing. arg0 = window_id, arg1..arg3 reserved (0). The reply carries arg1 = stride in bytes, arg2 = required byte size, arg3 = (width << 16) \| height, all for the window's current content extent.  The client then acquires a transfer buffer of at least that size, borrows it to the compositor, and names it with GFX_IPC_ATTACH_SURFACE. A resize bumps the window generation, so the spec must be re-read and a new surface attached rather than the attached one resized in place -- a borrowed buffer is never mutated (docs/architecture/12-dma-transfers.md).  This replaced a compositor-side allocation that granted the buffer to the caller: a server cannot own a buffer it hands to a client.  |
| `GFX_IPC_ATTACH_SURFACE` | 0x211 | req | Register a surface the CLIENT owns and has borrowed to the compositor. arg0 = window_id, arg1 = buffer_id, arg2 = borrow_id, arg3 reserved (0).  Three ids are a fixed, non-growing set, so they travel as bare argument words rather than a descriptor (skills/wasmos-add-opcode, Step 0). Both ids are required and neither is derivable compositor-side: xfer_buffer_borrow returns borrow_id to the OWNER, and the two are not interchangeable -- xfer_buffer_read/write key on buffer_id, while the borrow-side mapping path keys on borrow_id.  Attach registers a surface; GFX_IPC_PRESENT_WINDOW names which attached surface is ready. Keeping them separate is what lets a client hold two surfaces at once, which both resize and tear-free presentation need.  |
| `GFX_IPC_DETACH_SURFACE` | 0x212 | req | Withdraw a surface previously attached with GFX_IPC_ATTACH_SURFACE. arg0 = window_id, arg1 = buffer_id, arg2..arg3 reserved (0).  The client MUST detach before releasing the buffer. There is no unborrow notification, so a release while the compositor still holds the borrow leaves it reading a revoked borrow mid-composite; the acknowledged detach is that missing handshake. This replaced a call that asked the compositor to free a buffer the compositor owned.  |
| `GFX_IPC_RESP` | 0x280 | resp |  |
| `GFX_IPC_ERROR` | 0x2FF | error |  |

## pci (0xD00–0xDFF)

| Opcode | Value | Kind | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `PCI_IPC_MSI_QUERY` | 0xD00 | req | Ask what message-signalled interrupt support a PCI function has. arg0=bdf ((bus<<8)\|(device<<3)\|function) arg1..arg3=reserved(0). On success: PCI_IPC_RESP, arg0=WASMOS_PCI_MSI_KIND_* (MSIX preferred over MSI when both are present), arg1=number of vectors the device supports. On failure: PCI_IPC_ERROR, arg1=packed msi domain code.  |
| `PCI_IPC_MSI_BIND` | 0xD01 | req | Program one MSI/MSI-X table entry of a PCI function with an address/data pair the caller obtained from wasmos_msi_alloc, enable the capability, and set INTX_DISABLE so the device stops driving its shared INTx line. arg0=((bdf<<8)\|entry) arg1=address_lo arg2=address_hi arg3=data. On success: PCI_IPC_RESP, arg0=entry. On failure: PCI_IPC_ERROR, arg1=packed msi domain code.  |
| `PCI_IPC_MSI_UNBIND` | 0xD02 | req | Mask one MSI/MSI-X table entry again. Disables the whole capability when the last bound entry of the function is released. arg0=((bdf<<8)\|entry) arg1..arg3=reserved(0). On success: PCI_IPC_RESP, arg0=entry. On failure: PCI_IPC_ERROR, arg1=packed msi domain code.  |
| `PCI_IPC_BUS_MASTER_REQ` | 0xD03 | req | Turn bus mastering on for a PCI function, on behalf of its driver. arg0=bdf ((bus<<8)\|(device<<3)\|function) arg1..arg3=reserved(0). For a driver that takes no MSI and no INTx: an MSI bind and PCI_IPC_INTX_ENABLE_REQ turn bus mastering on themselves, and nothing else does once the kernel quiesced the function at a previous driver's end. The driver stops its own DMA engine before asking, since the device still names the previous driver's frames. Written through pci_config_write_for, so only the function's driver can arm it. On success: PCI_IPC_RESP, arg0=0. On failure: PCI_IPC_ERROR, arg1=WASMOS_ERR_MSI_BAD_DEVICE or WASMOS_ERR_MSI_NOT_FUNCTION_DRIVER.  |
| `PCI_IPC_INTX_ENABLE_REQ` | 0xD04 | req | Arm a PCI function for its INTx pin, on behalf of its driver: bus mastering on and INTX_DISABLE cleared. The INTx counterpart of PCI_IPC_MSI_BIND, for a driver that falls back to INTx; the kernel set INTX_DISABLE and cleared bus mastering when the function's previous driver ended, and nothing else undoes either. A later MSI bind sets INTX_DISABLE again. The driver resets the device before asking, since the device still names the previous driver's frames. arg0=bdf ((bus<<8)\|(device<<3)\|function) arg1..arg3=reserved(0). Written through pci_config_write_for, so only the function's driver can arm it. On success: PCI_IPC_RESP, arg0=0. On failure: PCI_IPC_ERROR, arg1=WASMOS_ERR_MSI_BAD_DEVICE or WASMOS_ERR_MSI_NOT_FUNCTION_DRIVER.  |
| `PCI_IPC_RESP` | 0xD80 | resp |  |
| `PCI_IPC_ERROR` | 0xDFF | error |  |

## system (0xFF02–0xFF85)

| Opcode | Value | Kind | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `WASMOS_IPC_SHUTDOWN_REQ` | 0xFF02 | req | The system is going down; quiesce and answer WASMOS_IPC_SHUTDOWN_DONE. arg0 = reason (0 = halt, 1 = reboot), arg1..arg3 reserved (0). Sent by the process manager, one at a time, to every registered driver and service that declared WASMOS_SVC_FLAG_WANTS_SHUTDOWN: each before everything it NEEDS by its manifest's [deps], directly or through processes that are not participants, so a participant still has the services beneath it while it quiesces; otherwise in reverse spawn order (docs/architecture/15-drivers-and-services.md, "Orderly Shutdown Design Direction"; src/kernel/include/shutdown_order.h). A participant that does not answer within the deadline is passed over and the machine still goes down, which is safe because of what the notification exists to do: a filesystem that misses it mounts read-only next boot rather than serving inconsistent metadata. This subsystem's range is above every other subsystem's because the message arrives on the PARTICIPANT's own endpoint, where a subsystem-scoped value would collide -- gfx and proc_manager both own 0x200. It is the band the kernel's IRQ (0xff00) and MSI (0xff01) events already use for the same reason; those two stay hand-written in src/drivers/include/wasmos_driver_abi.h and src/kernel/include/irq.h.  |
| `WASMOS_IPC_HANGUP` | 0xFF03 | notify | A process that was your peer has ended. arg0 = the endpoint of it that was your peer, or IPC_ENDPOINT_NONE when the context itself was watched; arg1 = the context that ended, which is what per-client state is keyed by; arg2..arg3 reserved (0). Several of a context's endpoints may each have been your peer, so one context can arrive more than once: releasing its state must be idempotent.  Delivered to the endpoints that ended process had actually SENT to, and to no others. That scoping is the point: a service that holds state on behalf of its clients -- a working directory, a socket, a window -- hears about its own clients ending and nothing else. There is no subscription, because the relationship the notification follows is the one the sends already created. Where a service holds state for a context at someone else's request, before that context sends it anything, the kernel-side requester watches the context instead (ipc_context_watch): the process manager does this when it has fs-manager copy a child's working directory.  Only the kernel sends it. ipc_send_from refuses this type from any guest context with IPC_ERR_PERM, because a receiver acts on it by releasing a client's state and a forged one would release a live client's.  A hangup is never refused and never lost to a full queue. Its record is allocated when it becomes owed, the last ring slot of every endpoint is filled only by hangups, and further hangups wait in the kernel and move into the ring as the receiver drains it -- always after every message queued before them, so a client's last requests are served before its state is released.  A dead endpoint tracks a bounded number of destinations (IPC_ENDPOINT_CONTACTS_MAX). A client that talked to more services than that, or whose record could not be allocated, leaves the untracked ones unnotified, which is a leak rather than an error; the reap reports it on the serial console.  |
| `WASMOS_IPC_KMSG_NOTIFY` | 0xFF04 | notify | kernel -> kmsg subscriber: kernel log has been appended since the last notify. Fire-and-forget, no payload (arg0..arg3 = 0): the subscriber pages the ring with kmsg_read from where it stopped, so one notify covers any number of appends and none is owed per line. Sent from the scheduler loop, never from the logging path, to the endpoint passed to kmsg_subscribe. In this band because it arrives on the SUBSCRIBER's own endpoint, like WASMOS_IPC_HANGUP.  |
| `WASMOS_IPC_HEALTH_REQ` | 0xFF05 | req | Liveness probe: is this event loop turning? Answered with WASMOS_IPC_HEALTH_RESP and the request's request_id by the event loop itself -- wasmos_sys_event_loop_poll, wasmos_sys_native_event_loop_poll and the AssemblyScript EventLoop -- before intents and handlers, so service code never sees it. arg0..arg3 reserved (0). The answer proves exactly what a supervisor needs to know: a loop parked in a nested receive, or stuck in a handler, does not answer. A supervisor probes only a unit that named its loop endpoint in PROC_IPC_NOTIFY_READY (PROC_READY_FLAG_LIVENESS); a service with a hand-written receive loop does not answer and must not opt in. In this band because it arrives on the unit's own endpoint.  |
| `WASMOS_IPC_SHUTDOWN_DONE` | 0xFF82 | resp | Sent back to the process manager when a participant has quiesced. arg0..arg3 reserved (0). Answering does not mean the participant stops running; it means nothing it holds still needs to reach a device.  |
| `WASMOS_IPC_HEALTH_RESP` | 0xFF85 | resp | The answer to WASMOS_IPC_HEALTH_REQ, from the probed endpoint, with the probe's request_id. arg0..arg3 = 0.  |

## volume (0xE00–0xEFF)

| Opcode | Value | Kind | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `VOLUME_IPC_IDENTIFY_REQ` | 0xE00 | req | Ask the volume manager to describe one volume into a buffer the CALLER owns. arg0 = the volume's `volume` CLASS INSTANCE, arg1 = buffer_id. Answered with VOLUME_IPC_IDENTIFY_RESP.  Same ownership as BLOCK_IPC_IDENTIFY_REQ, and for the same reason: the caller acquires the buffer and borrows it to this endpoint with WRITE, because the client of a request owns the buffer and the server is a transient grantee (architecture/12-dma-transfers.md).  What a caller wants from this is usually `backing_instance`: a volume is not something you read from, it is something that tells you which `block` device to read from. The volume manager is deliberately not in the I/O path.  |
| `VOLUME_IPC_CLAIM_REQ` | 0xE01 | req | Record that the sender has mounted a volume, or release that record. arg0 = the volume's class instance, arg1 = 1 to claim and 0 to release. Answered with VOLUME_IPC_RESP, arg0 = 0.  RECORDS a claim; does not enforce one. The volume manager is not in the I/O path, so a tool that does not ask is not stopped -- this is what `fsck` and `mkfs` consult before touching a volume that may be mounted, and enforcing it would mean standing in the data path for every read to prevent a mistake only those two can make.  |
| `VOLUME_IPC_RESCAN_REQ` | 0xE02 | req | Re-probe a block device and update the volume on it. arg0 = the device's `block` CLASS INSTANCE -- the device, not the volume, because a caller that has just written a filesystem knows which disk it wrote and a volume for it may not exist yet. Answered with VOLUME_IPC_RESP, arg0 = 0, arg1 = 1 when a volume is present on the device afterwards and 0 when none was recognised.  A device is probed once, when it arrives under the `block` class, and nothing re-probes it afterwards -- so a disk formatted from inside the guest keeps whatever the volume manager saw on it at boot, and every rule and tool that reads the volume layer sees the stale answer. This is what `mkfs` sends once its write has landed.  The reply is DEFERRED: a probe is synchronous and runs on the volume manager's root task, so the request is queued and answered when that probe completes rather than from the handler that received it.  Updates the volume IN PLACE, keeping its class instance -- which is a fingerprint of a canonical id derived from the device, so it does not change -- and keeping any CLAIM on it, which belongs to whoever holds the volume and not to the probe.  |
| `VOLUME_IPC_IDENTIFY_RESP` | 0xE80 | resp | arg0 = 0, arg1 = bytes written into the caller's buffer. |
| `VOLUME_IPC_RESP` | 0xE81 | resp |  |
| `VOLUME_IPC_ERROR` | 0xEFF | error | arg0 = packed error code. |

## partition (0xF00–0xFFF)

| Opcode | Value | Kind | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `PARTITION_IPC_RESCAN_REQ` | 0xF00 | req | Re-read one disk's partition table and reconcile what is published against what it now says. arg0 = the DISK's `block` class instance -- the backing device, never a partition of it, because a caller that has just written a table knows which disk it wrote and the partitions it describes may not exist yet. Answered with PARTITION_IPC_RESP, arg0 = 0, arg1 = the partition count on that disk afterwards.  A disk's table is read once, when the disk arrives under the `block` class, and nothing re-reads it afterwards -- so a table rewritten from inside the guest leaves every partition device as it was at boot. This is what `fdisk` sends once its write has landed.  Reconciled, not republished. A partition whose window is unchanged is left strictly alone, beyond restating a descriptor whose METADATA moved -- a label, a type GUID, a PARTUUID -- which moves no storage. Re-registering its class would disturb a filesystem mounted on it to no purpose.  A partition whose WINDOW changed keeps its class instance -- a fingerprint of an id derived from the disk and the slot, so it does not move -- and only its descriptor is restated. A partition the new table no longer holds is RETIRED: withdrawn from the device manager's inventory first, and unregistered from the `block` class only once that succeeded.  Both of those are gated on the same question, because both are unsafe under a live mount. A retirement makes the device unfindable while a filesystem is still writing to it; a window change redirects those writes, since every forwarded transfer is rebased onto the window and clamped to it.  The question is put to FS-MANAGER, which brokers every mount and names each one's backing device by canonical id. Nothing else can answer it: the device manager's inventory cannot, and the volume manager's CLAIM covers only devices it managed to recognise a filesystem on -- a partition whose probe failed carries no volume, mounts perfectly well anyway, and would read as unheld. Any answer that is not a mount table is "cannot tell" and refuses.  A refusal leaves the partition exactly as it was. arg2 counts every partition the rescan could not reconcile -- a change refused, a change that could not be started, or an addition with no free slot -- rather than failing the whole request, because the other partitions of the disk were reconciled correctly and the caller needs to know how much did not take.  The reply is DEFERRED: reading a table is synchronous and runs on the partition manager's root task, and the retirements it schedules are answered by their own peers later still, so the request is queued and answered when all of that has settled.  |
| `PARTITION_IPC_RESP` | 0xF80 | resp | arg0 = 0, arg1 = partitions on the disk after the rescan, arg2 = partitions the rescan could not reconcile. |
| `PARTITION_IPC_ERROR` | 0xFFF | error | arg0 = packed error code. |

## supervisor (0x1000–0x10FF)

| Opcode | Value | Kind | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `SUPERVISOR_IPC_SUBMIT_REQ` | 0x1000 | req | Hand a unit to the supervisor, which spawns it, watches it and restarts it by its policy. The sender must hold svc.control (WASMOS_ERR_SUPERVISOR_NOT_AUTHORIZED). The request is a wasmos_supervisor_submit_desc_t in a transfer buffer the caller owns and has lent READ to the supervisor: arg0=buffer_id arg1=offset arg2=size. Its spec is one line of text:   <unit> <path> [restart=never\|on-failure\|always]                 [class=optional\|required\|critical] [tty=<slot>]                 [probe=<seconds>] [parent=<unit>] [-- <args>] <unit> is template or template@instance; the instance key names what the unit serves (a tty, a device) and survives a restart. parent binds the unit to a unit already held (WASMOS_ERR_SUPERVISOR_NO_PARENT otherwise), for a unit whose state cannot outlive its parent's instance: when the parent's instance ends and another follows, the unit's running instance is killed and respawned at once; when the parent stops or is given up on, the unit is stopped and held degraded. Neither end counts against the unit's restart limit; a critical unit stopped this way takes the system down. A unit that can rebind to a restarted peer needs no parent. tty pins a wants_tty unit to text slot 1 or above; slot 0 is the kernel log and is refused. probe is the liveness probe period, 1-999 s (default 10 s), both stretched by kenv supervisor.timescale. It applies only to an instance whose READY names its event-loop endpoint (PROC_READY_FLAG_LIVENESS); three probes unanswered in a row and the supervisor kills the instance as a failure. The descriptor may also carry a capability descriptor (wasmos_spawn_caps_v2_t, I/O windows and IRQ lines), which every spawn of the unit carries. Grants are relayed only from a submitter that also holds spawn.grant (WASMOS_ERR_SUPERVISOR_GRANT_NOT_AUTHORIZED); a unit asking for DMA must name its PCI function (DEVMGR_CAP_PCI_FUNCTION), which the kernel quiesces whenever the instance ends, or it is refused (WASMOS_ERR_SUPERVISOR_DMA_CAPS). Answered once the unit is accepted, before it is spawned: a spawn that fails later is the unit's failure, handled by its policy.  |
| `SUPERVISOR_IPC_LIST_REQ` | 0x1001 | req | Report every unit the supervisor holds; open to every sender. The request is a wasmos_supervisor_list_desc_t followed by room for `capacity` wasmos_supervisor_unit_record_t, in a transfer buffer the caller owns and has lent READ\|WRITE to the supervisor: arg0=buffer_id arg1=offset arg2=size, where size covers the records. The supervisor writes up to `capacity` records in table order, then `total` (units held) and `count` (records written) into the descriptor, and answers. count < total means the room was short; SUPERVISOR_UNITS_MAX records are always enough.  |
| `SUPERVISOR_IPC_BOOT_SUBMITTED_REQ` | 0x1002 | req | Every unit of the boot set has been submitted: sent by sysinit when sysinit.rc has run to its end; the sender must hold svc.control (WASMOS_ERR_SUPERVISOR_NOT_AUTHORIZED). arg0..arg3 reserved (0). The units the supervisor holds at that moment are the boot set, and the boot milestone is decided over them: once every required (or critical) one is up -- READY and, if probed, a probe answered -- the supervisor logs "[supervisor] boot complete at <ms> ms: <n> required units up" once; if one of them fails or stops first, it logs "[supervisor] boot failed: <unit> ..." once instead. A unit submitted later is not part of the boot set. Answered at once; a second one changes nothing.  |
| `SUPERVISOR_IPC_KILL_REQ` | 0x1003 | req | Kill a unit's running instance. The sender must hold svc.control (WASMOS_ERR_SUPERVISOR_NOT_AUTHORIZED). The request is a wasmos_supervisor_unit_desc_t naming the unit, in a transfer buffer the caller owns and has lent READ to the supervisor: arg0=buffer_id arg1=offset arg2=size. The instance must be spawned and not already being killed (starting, running or stable); otherwise the request is refused with WASMOS_ERR_SUPERVISOR_NOT_RUNNING, and with WASMOS_ERR_SUPERVISOR_NO_UNIT when no unit has that name. The end of a killed instance is a failure, handled by the unit's policy like any other: an on-failure or always unit is restarted, a never unit is given up, and a critical unit's end takes the system down. Answered once the kill is sent to the process manager, before the instance has ended; arg1 of the reply is the pid killed.  |
| `SUPERVISOR_IPC_RETRACT_REQ` | 0x1004 | req | Withdraw a unit, and every unit bound to it through parent=, from the supervisor: each running instance is killed, nothing is restarted, and no end counts as a failure. The sender must hold svc.control (WASMOS_ERR_SUPERVISOR_NOT_AUTHORIZED). The request is a wasmos_supervisor_unit_desc_t naming the unit, in a transfer buffer the caller owns and has lent READ to the supervisor: arg0=buffer_id arg1=offset arg2=size. Refused with WASMOS_ERR_SUPERVISOR_NO_UNIT when no unit has that name, and with WASMOS_ERR_SUPERVISOR_CRITICAL when the unit or one bound to it is critical. Answered once the kills are sent; arg1 of the reply is the pid killed for the named unit, 0 when it had no instance and was removed at once. A unit with an instance keeps its name until that instance has ended, so a submission of the same name is refused (EXISTS) until then.  |
| `SUPERVISOR_IPC_STOP_REQ` | 0x1005 | req | Stop a unit: its instance is killed and not restarted, its end does not count as a failure, and the unit stays recorded as stopped until SUPERVISOR_IPC_START_REQ or SUPERVISOR_IPC_RETRACT_REQ. Units bound to it through parent= are stopped and held degraded. The sender must hold svc.control (WASMOS_ERR_SUPERVISOR_NOT_AUTHORIZED). The request is a wasmos_supervisor_unit_desc_t naming the unit, in a transfer buffer the caller owns and has lent READ to the supervisor: arg0=buffer_id arg1=offset arg2=size. A unit waiting for its spawn or restart is stopped at once; one being spawned or killed is stopped when that settles. Refused with WASMOS_ERR_SUPERVISOR_NO_UNIT when no unit has that name, WASMOS_ERR_SUPERVISOR_NOT_RUNNING when it is already stopped, failed or degraded, and WASMOS_ERR_SUPERVISOR_CRITICAL when it or a unit bound to it is critical. Answered once the kill is sent; arg1 of the reply is the pid killed, 0 when the unit had no running instance.  |
| `SUPERVISOR_IPC_START_REQ` | 0x1006 | req | Start a stopped, failed or degraded unit: it is spawned as if newly submitted, with its backoff and its intensity window cleared, so a unit that gave up can be brought back. Its restart count is kept. Units bound to it through parent= and held degraded start with it. The sender must hold svc.control (WASMOS_ERR_SUPERVISOR_NOT_AUTHORIZED). The request is a wasmos_supervisor_unit_desc_t naming the unit, in a transfer buffer the caller owns and has lent READ to the supervisor: arg0=buffer_id arg1=offset arg2=size. Refused with WASMOS_ERR_SUPERVISOR_NO_UNIT when no unit has that name, WASMOS_ERR_SUPERVISOR_RUNNING when it is not stopped, failed or degraded, and WASMOS_ERR_SUPERVISOR_PARENT_DOWN when its parent is. Answered once the spawn is due, before the instance runs.  |
| `SUPERVISOR_IPC_RESP` | 0x1080 | resp | arg0 = 0: the unit was accepted, the list was written, the boot set was recorded, the kill, retraction or stop was sent (arg1 = the pid, 0 for a unit without an instance), or the start is due. |
| `SUPERVISOR_IPC_ERROR` | 0x10FF | error | arg0 = packed WASMOS_ERR_SUPERVISOR_* code. |

## display (0x1100–0x11FF)

| Opcode | Value | Kind | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `DISPLAY_IPC_FLUSH_REQ` | 0x1100 | req | Present what was drawn into the scanout inside the given rectangles. The request is a wasmos_display_flush_desc_t (version, count, rects in framebuffer pixels) in a transfer buffer the caller owns and has lent READ to the display: arg0=buffer_id arg1=offset arg2=size. The caller may rewrite the buffer once the answer arrives, so damage drawn meanwhile is accumulated, not sent. Rects are clipped to the scanout; an empty list presents nothing. Served by the endpoint registered as "display", which exists only on a machine whose scanout needs a presenter (virtio-gpu); elsewhere what is drawn is already shown.  |
| `DISPLAY_IPC_RESP` | 0x1180 | resp | arg0 = 0: the rects were presented; the descriptor buffer is the caller's again. |
| `DISPLAY_IPC_ERROR` | 0x11FF | error | arg0 = packed WASMOS_ERR_DISPLAY_* code; the descriptor buffer is the caller's again. |

## keyring (0x1200–0x12FF)

| Opcode | Value | Kind | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `KEYRING_IPC_ALLOW_REQ` | 0x1200 | req | Let a package start although its signature is verified by no trusted key ("start anyway"): it then runs from bytecode with ipc.basic only. The payload is the package's SHA-512 digest (64 bytes) followed by its path (up to 128 bytes, not NUL-terminated, recorded beside the digest), in a transfer buffer the caller owns and has lent READ to the keyring: arg0=buffer_id arg1=offset arg2=size. Requires keyring.admin. The digest is registered with the kernel and appended to /boot/system/keys/allow.lst before the answer.  |
| `KEYRING_IPC_ADD_KEY_REQ` | 0x1201 | req | Trust a publisher's key: the payload is a PEM "PUBLIC KEY" file (Ed25519, or RSA of 2048 to 4096 bits; at most 4096 bytes) in a transfer buffer the caller owns and has lent READ to the keyring: arg0=buffer_id arg1=offset arg2=size. Requires keyring.admin. The key is registered with the kernel and written to /boot/system/keys/<first 8 hex digits of its id>.pem before the answer.  |
| `KEYRING_IPC_RESP` | 0x1280 | resp | arg0 = 0: the change is in force and recorded; the payload buffer is the caller's again. |
| `KEYRING_IPC_ERROR` | 0x12FF | error | arg0 = packed WASMOS_ERR_KEYRING_* code, or the kernel's WASMOS_ERR_KERNEL_* refusal; the payload buffer is the caller's again. |
